newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia trade balance swings to deficit in March.
newsitem.headline: Australia trade balance swings to deficit in March.

text.p: Data released on Wednesday showed Australia's volatile monthly trade balance swung sharply into deficit during March, with a large fall in exports the key to a deterioration which came in well below market expectations.

The Australian Bureau of Statistics said the balance of goods and services was in deficit by A$103 million in March, a big turnaround on the A$315 million surplus in February and well below the median forecast of a A$150 million surplus.

"The reversal, from a surplus to a deficit, of the balance of goods and services should be viewed with a degree and caution," Nomura Australia economists said, pointing to the series volatility. The balance has alternated between surplus and deficit over the last six months.
Exports of goods and services fell by A$664 million, or 7.3 percent, in March while imports of goods and services fell by A$246 million, or 2.8 percent.
Exports were expected to be weaker after a strong patch in late 1996 and early 1997 but the size of the fall surprised many economists.

"To the extent that the deterioration in March was led by a 10.4 percent drop in rural exports, today's figures should probably be seen as an inevitable correction from some unusually good results in late 1996/early 1997," Commonwealth Bank economist Micheal Blythe said.
The data had little market impact given the monthly volatility and the fact that the market is still familiarising itself with the report, which is now in its third month.

Despite the sharp turnaround in March, the data pointed to an improvement in the first quarter current account and net exports were expected to be a positive contributor to first quarter economic growth.
However, with prospects of stronger domestic growth through 1997 expected to lead to increased import demand, the balance could deteriorate through the year.

"Further out, as we move through 1997, we see the current account deteriorating as the economy gains momentum and lifts imports and as the boost from record grain exports drops out of the numbers," Westpac senior economist John Peters said.
